title: About
text:
What drives me
I’m interested in how environmental sustainability and emerging technologies shape social and behavioral health outcomes. That means asking who the technology serves, who absorbs its externalities, and what it would take to shift that balance. Long term, I want to bring these tools into orthopedic and sports medicine care, and to build a health equity center in my own community.

title: Projects
text:
Energy Burden, Air Quality, and Health in Atlanta
A sustainability project with Georgia Power under the Health Solutions Advisement Group, examining how energy choices shape air quality and health outcomes across Atlanta’s neighborhood planning units. The work focuses on NPU T and NPU V, tracking asthma as the primary respiratory link alongside diabetes and cancer as secondary burdens, from 2020 to 2026. The framework traces the pathway from historical drivers like redlining and housing disinvestment through present-day energy burden and air quality exposure, and back again through reinvestment and policy.







Causal pathway linking historical disinvestment to energy burden, air quality exposure, and health outcomes in Atlanta NPUs T and V




More Than A Run Club Health Survey Initiative
A community health survey initiative built around a run club in Atlanta. My role is developing the survey questions alongside the data collection team and running the analysis once the collection window closes. The survey runs from late September through October 31.

title: Be The Change You Wanna See
text:
I’m a Master of Public Health student at Morehouse School of Medicine working at the intersection of data science, public health, and applied research. My goal is to translate complex data into insights people can actually use.


I believe change is possible, and that data science, health equity, and systems-level thinking are among the sharpest tools we have for reducing the disparities communities face worldwide.
Right now, my work explores how data can help us understand the social, environmental, and structural factors that shape health outcomes from energy burden and air quality in Atlanta neighborhoods to how AI infrastructure gets sited in the communities least equipped to absorb its costs.
What I’m building toward is simple. Communities should have the resources to care for their own health and our systems should be built around preventing illness, not just treating it.



If you’re working on applied data science in healthcare or advancing equitable health outcomes, I’d like to hear about it.

title: Research
text:
As AI infrastructure expands, data centers are being placed in neighborhoods that have little say in the decision and little visibility into the environmental and health consequences that follow.


The public health concerns cluster into four areas:
Water. Large facilities draw heavily on local water for cooling, competing with residential and agricultural demand in watersheds that may already be stressed.However a lot of big tech companies claim to invest in those local watersheds.
Energy sourcing. Rapid load growth is being met in part by extending the life of fossil generation or bringing on new gas capacity, which shifts the question from how much power a facility uses to what that power is made of and who breathes the byproducts.
Emissions accounting. Scope 2 emissions those tied to purchased electricity often fall outside the boundaries of local environmental review even though they represent the bulk of a facility’s carbon footprint. Greenhouse gas contributions and localized air quality effects from backup diesel generation are similarly under-captured.
Facility design. Where a facility is placed, how it’s cooled, where the generators sit, setback distance, and noise attenuation all shape how much of the burden lands on adjacent residents. These are design decisions, which means they could be negotiable decisions.



The review follows JBI scoping review methodology, structured through the PCC framework and paired with stakeholder mapping to identify where communities hold real leverage in the siting and approval process.
Because the regulatory landscape is moving faster than the peer-reviewed literature, the review deliberately incorporates grey literature: executive orders, state accountability frameworks, permit filings, utility resource plans, and local land use records. Virginia’s Executive Order 22, signed September 18, 2026, illustrates why this matters. It establishes a statewide Data Center Accountability Framework, bars executive branch agencies from entering non-disclosure agreements on data center projects, replaces by-right approval with public hearing requirements for projects above 25 megawatts, and directs agencies to develop standards for emissions, water use, and energy costs.
That order is the clearest signal yet that the transparency gap this model addresses is being recognized at the state level and it arrived through policy channels, not journals.



Status: [scoping review in progress]
Methods: JBI scoping review, PCC framework, stakeholder mapping
Output: [manuscript / portable framework / presentation]
